chunks.text: Solid medicines have to disintegrate and dissolve before they can be absorbed, and most oral medicines are absorbed in the proximal jejunum, so many can be used in short bowel syndrome; sustained-release and delayed-release medicines, however, should be avoided.

diagram.label: Guidance says to avoid sustained- and delayed-release forms after major resection

chunks.text: When applicable, other ways of giving a medicine, such as liquids or topical forms, should be considered in short bowel syndrome. If a medicine is not working, the options include a different formulation or a different route, such as intravenous, subcutaneous or transdermal.
Monitoring medication levels in the blood should be considered in short bowel syndrome.
Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel, so many medicines can still be used in short bowel syndrome when they are not sustained- or delayed-release forms.

diagram.label: Most medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel

chunks.text: By whether colon remains, short bowel syndrome is classified into three groups: end-jejunostomy; jejunum joined to part of the colon (jejunocolonic); and jejuno-ileo-colic, keeping the whole colon and the ileocecal valve. The end-jejunostomy group is the most severe.

A remaining small-bowel length of 200 cm or less is generally agreed to meet criteria for short bowel syndrome. People without a colon who have under 100 cm of jejunum tend to be net secretors, losing more water and sodium from the stoma than they take in by mouth.
chunks.section: Introduction; Best Practice Advice 5: Oral Rehydration Solution

chunks.text: In short bowel syndrome, hypertonic drinks such as fruit juices and sodas should be limited to reduce output, particularly with net secretion and a high-output jejunostomy.

diagram.label: Water and sodium handling differs along the small bowel

chunks.section: Best Practice Advice 5: Oral Rehydration Solution

chunks.text: In short bowel syndrome, low-sodium hypotonic drinks such as water, tea, coffee and alcohol should be limited to reduce output, particularly with net secretion and a high-output jejunostomy; drinking large quantities of water generally increases ostomy output.
chunks.section: Best Practice Advice 5: Oral Rehydration Solution

chunks.text: Instead of large amounts of water, a glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution (ORS) is preferred in short bowel syndrome to enhance absorption and reduce secretion, because glucose in the gut stimulates sodium absorption, which water follows.

diagram.label: Glucose and sodium together help the small bowel absorb water

chunks.section: Best Practice Advice 5: Oral Rehydration Solution

chunks.text: Oral rehydration solutions differ from commercial sports drinks: an ORS has considerably more sodium and less sugar.
chunks.section: Best Practice Advice 5: Oral Rehydration Solution

chunks.text: In short bowel syndrome, the larger amount of food that is needed is best tolerated spread through the day over several meals.
Diet in short bowel syndrome should focus on maintaining compensatory hyperphagia (eating more than estimated needs) rather than on excessive dietary restrictions, guided by an experienced dietitian.
With the colon in continuity, a diet high in complex carbohydrates and relatively low in fat is advised; it tends to reduce calorie loss in stool and improve energy absorption.

diagram.label: With a colon, a diet high in complex carbohydrates improves energy absorption

chunks.text: People with an end-jejunostomy do not appear to benefit from fat restriction; more fat is absorbed when more is eaten.
With a colon, oxalate restriction (for example peanuts and baked beans) is essential for people at risk of high urinary oxalate and oxalate kidney stones.

Antidiarrheal medicines that slow the gut, such as loperamide, are commonly used to control stool losses in short bowel syndrome; loperamide is preferred to opiate drugs, and their use should be guided by objective measurements of stool output.

Massive bowel resection is associated with gastric acid hypersecretion that may last 6 to 12 months; acid-suppressing medicines such as proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers are beneficial in reducing gastric secretions. It has been suggested they be used sparingly beyond 12 months unless there is clear benefit.
People with short bowel syndrome should be taught to measure their daily urine output; urine output, stool or ostomy output, weight and complaints of thirst are watched to guide fluid needs.
chunks.section: Best Practice Advice 2: Nutrition Assessment; Best Practice Advice 4: PN

chunks.text: Time-release formulations, such as extended-release or controlled-release tablets, are designed to make the drug available for absorption over an extended period, especially in the small intestine.

diagram.label: Time-release designs release the drug over time, mainly in the small intestine

chunks.section: Understanding the Implications of Drug Formulations

chunks.text: After extensive resection, sustained-release or extended-release products should generally be avoided, because the extent of drug absorption can be erratic or severely impaired.
chunks.section: Understanding the Implications of Drug Formulations

chunks.text: Delayed-release and enteric-coated tablets have a coating that delays disintegration and dissolution until the tablet has passed through the stomach.
chunks.section: Understanding the Implications of Drug Formulations

chunks.text: For people whose upper gut was resected, liquid forms such as oral solutions or suspensions can improve absorption, but sugar alcohols such as sorbitol and xylitol in them can make diarrhea worse. People with short bowel syndrome rarely have had upper-gut resections.
chunks.section: Understanding the Implications of Drug Formulations

chunks.text: If a medicine is not working in short bowel syndrome, the care team may consider changing its formulation (for example a crushed tablet, a capsule or a liquid) or its route.
Sugar alcohols such as sorbitol and xylitol, found as inactive ingredients in some medicines, can make diarrhea worse in short bowel syndrome.
chunks.section: Understanding the Implications of Drug Formulations; Table 2

chunks.text: In short bowel syndrome, malabsorption of a medicine is an important consideration, particularly when the expected response to it is not seen.

Proton pump inhibitors are the primary medicines used as maintenance therapy for gastric acid hypersecretion in short bowel syndrome. All oral proton pump inhibitors have an enteric coating, so their absorption may be limited in short bowel syndrome; if an oral one is not working early after surgery, a trial of an intravenous one is reasonable.

Drinking large quantities of water is a major misconception in short bowel syndrome; patients, particularly those with an end jejunostomy, may benefit from a glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution instead.
Most people with short bowel syndrome who have a colon can usually stay adequately hydrated with hypotonic fluids without excessive fluid loss.

diagram.label: With a colon, most people stay hydrated with ordinary fluids

chunks.text: The optimal sodium concentration of an oral rehydration solution in short bowel syndrome is 90 to 120 mmol/L (mEq/L); the clinician decides who needs one from urine output, low blood pressure, recurrent dehydration and kidney injury.

Salty snacks are encouraged in short bowel syndrome, and liberal use of salt can help replace the sodium lost in stool; the diet guidelines say to increase salt without a colon and keep usual intake with a colon.

In short bowel syndrome, simple sugars and sugar alcohols are limited in both foods and fluids; sodas, fruit juices, fruit drinks and sweet teas are avoided because the sugar in these drinks is related to how much output follows.
Fat restriction is most important in short bowel syndrome with a remaining colon, severe steatorrhea or a history of oxalate kidney stones.
In short bowel syndrome, lactose may be tolerated and does not always need to be avoided.

In this study, oral formulations were grouped by risk in ostomy patients: noncritical (accelerated release, such as chewable or effervescent tablets, granules and liquids), potentially critical (regular release, such as coated tablets and hard capsules) and critical (modified release, such as enteric-coated, matrix and prolonged-release products).
chunks.section: Methods: Classification of drugs according to their formulation (Table 1)

chunks.text: Medicine seen in the ostomy bag can be undissolved, or it can be a tablet shell or insoluble matrix that often remains after the drug has been released; a medicine can also dissolve fully and still not be fully absorbed because transit is short. Seeing it does not show on its own whether the medicine worked.

In the interviews, 11 of 50 ostomy patients reported seeing undissolved medicine or indigestible material in their stoma bag at least once, and more than 60% said they lacked information that this could happen.
People with a colostomy are unlikely to have significant problems with drug absorption, because most drugs are absorbed in the small intestine; usual formulations can be used for most of them.

In most cases a stoma is not the main factor in drug absorption; absorption correlates with the length of small intestine remaining, and with a jejunostomy or ileostomy, using medicines normally depends largely on that remaining length.
Although drugs can be absorbed along the whole gut, most drug absorption happens in the upper small intestine, where the long villi increase the surface area.

diagram.label: Most drug absorption happens in the upper small intestine

chunks.section: Drug absorption in the gastrointestinal tract

chunks.text: The large intestine has a minimal role in drug absorption, mainly limited to slow-release drugs and drugs that act in the large intestine.

diagram.label: Slow-release products can rely on the colon for part of their absorption

chunks.section: Drug absorption in the gastrointestinal tract

chunks.text: When poor absorption is suspected, liquids, capsules and uncoated tablets are likely to be better absorbed, and it may be necessary to avoid modified-release (slow-, controlled- or sustained-release) or enteric-coated formulations.

Before using a liquid medicine, its osmolarity, inactive ingredients and volume should be considered: high-osmolarity liquids can cause osmotic diarrhoea, and products containing sorbitol can in theory cause diarrhoea.
If a solid dose form is altered, for example crushed or opened, its tolerability or efficacy can change, so checking the product information or asking a pharmacist is recommended.
Proton pump inhibitors are often used in people with a short gut to reduce the volume of upper gut secretions.
Some medicines have effects that can be monitored, such as heart rate for beta blockers or the INR for warfarin, and some have blood levels that can be measured, such as digoxin and lithium.
Across 50 studies of 37 drugs in short bowel syndrome, decreased absorption was found for 29 drugs, 6 of which lost their therapeutic effect.

The effect of short bowel syndrome on drug absorption appears to be drug-specific and to depend on the location and extent of resection; therapeutic drug monitoring, where available, should be considered, especially for drugs with narrow therapeutic indices.
A colon in continuity can contribute significantly to the absorption of some drugs (for example metoprolol), and drugs absorbed in the colon or over a wide window are least likely to be malabsorbed.

WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS contains sodium 75 mmol/L, chloride 65, glucose 75, potassium 20 and citrate 10 mmol/L (total 245 mOsm/L). It was designed for acute diarrhea, and its sodium is below the 90 to 120 mmol/L range given for short bowel syndrome.
Oral rehydration solution works because glucose and sodium are absorbed together in the small bowel, carrying water with them.

diagram.label: Glucose and sodium carry water in together in the small bowel

chunks.text: Signs of dehydration include urine darker than pale yellow, urinating less often, thirst, dry mouth, fatigue, lightheadedness or dizziness when standing, rapid weight loss, and stool output higher than total fluid intake; people with high output or symptoms of dehydration are asked to contact their doctor.
